svg.title: Uniform INT4 versus NF4 level placement under a Gaussian weight density
svg.desc: A normal density is drawn over the normalized range minus one to plus one. Below it, symmetric INT4 places fifteen evenly spaced levels, five of which fall inside the high-density core. NF4 places sixteen quantile-spaced levels, seven of which fall inside the same core, spending its code points where the weights actually are.
svg.text: Sixteen code points, two ways to spend them
Pretrained weights in a block are close to zero-mean Gaussian. After absmax scaling, ±1 is roughly ±2.5σ.
Only 5 of the 15 levels land in the core, and the 16th code (−8) is never used. Most of the resolution is spent on the sparsely populated tails.
7 of the 16 levels land in the core, every code point is used, and zero is still represented exactly so that padding and pruned weights stay exact.
NF4 levels are midpoints between quantiles of a standard normal, so each of the 16 codes receives roughly equal probability mass under the assumed density.
Both formats still store a per-block scale. NF4 is not fewer bits — it is a better allocation of the same 16 code points, and only for weights that really are Gaussian.
